body.p: Applicant submits this Reply in response to the Office Action mailed June 4, 2024.
I. Status of the Claims

By this Reply, Applicant amends claims 1, 7, 9, 15, and 17. The originally filed specification and drawings fully support the subject matter of the amended and new claims. Claims 1-20 are pending in this application. Claims 1, 9, and 17 are the sole independent claims.
II. Interview
Applicant thanks Examiner Kretzer for the courtesies extended during the

telephonic interview of August 27, 2024. The remarks provided below are consistent with the issues discussed and agreements reached during the interview. In particular, for the reasons provided below, the Examiner agreed that the pending objections and rejections of the claims would likely be overcome based on the amended claims and remarks resented herein, pending further search and consideration. III. Objection to the Claims

In the Office Action, claims 1, 9, and 17 were objected to for minor informalities. (Office Action at page 3.) These informalities have been addressed as suggested in the Office Action. Based on this, Applicant requests reconsideration of the claim objections. IV. Section 112(a) Rejections
In the Office Action, claims 1-20 were rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) for allegedly failing to comply with the written description requirement. (Office Action at pages 4-7.)
First, with respect to the feature:
determining a blood flow demand of the portion of the
patient's bowel modeled by the non-invasive patient-specific
anatomical model, based on a determined mass of the
portion of the patient's bowel, amount of visceral vasculature
and collateral pathway(s) supplying blood to the portion of
patient's bowel modeled by the non-invasive patient-specific anatomic model, and the received physiological state of the
patient
the Office Action asserts that the present specification does not disclose:
" determining a blood flow demand based on an amount of visceral
vasculature and collateral pathway(s) supplying blood to the portion of patient's bowel modeled by the noninvasive patient-specific anatomic
model (Office Action at page 4), and
" all three of the variables being used in conjunction to determine the blood
flow demand, as required by the claims (Office Action at page 5).

Applicant does not agree that the noted portions of the claims lack sufficient written support in the present specification. However, in the interest of advancing prosecution, the claims are amended herein to recite:

SVG {EMBED HERE} 1.504.333
c
y
These features find support in at least paragraph [0035] of the present specification as published. In view of this, Applicant requests that these § 112 rejections be withdrawn.
In addition, the Office Action asserts with respect to the above features and the features:
calculating a blood flow characteristic of blood delivered to
the portion of the patient's bowel using the determined blood flow demand and a value of microvascular resistance based
on the received physiological state

that "it is not clear what steps the processor has to perform in order for a processor to perform the claimed steps" and that the present specification "does not disclose the computer, processor, or generic computer components and the algorithm (e.g., the necessary steps and/or flowcharts) in regard to a processor performing the claimed functions in sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at the time of filing." (Office Action at page 6, emphasis added.) Here, the Office Action misstates the requirements for written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a).

The purpose of the adequate written description requirement is to ensure that the inventor had possession of the claimed subject matter at the time the application was filed. See M.P.E.P. § 2163. If a person of ordinary skill in the art would have understood the inventor to have been in possession of the claimed invention at the time of the filing, even if every nuance of the claims is not explicitly described in the specification, then the adequate written description requirement is met. In re Alton, 76 F.3d 1168, 1175, 37 U.S.P.Q.2d 1578, 1581 (Fed. Cir. 1996). The written description requirement may be satisfied using words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas. See M.P.E.P. § 2163(I) (citing Lockwood v. American Airlines, Inc., 107 F.3d 1565, 1572, 41 USPQ2d 1961, 1966 (Fed. Cir. 1997)). Indeed, in some circumstances, "drawings alone may provide a 'written description' of an invention as required by §112."
Vas-Cath, Inc. v. Mahurkar, 935 F.2d 1555, 1565, 19 USPQ2d 1111, 1118 (Fed. Cir. 1991).
Additionally, "[t]he examiner has the initial burden of presenting by a

preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in an applicant's disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims." See M.P.E.P. § 2163(III)(A). In rejecting claims under Section 112, first paragraph, the examiner "must set forth express findings of fact regarding the [] analysis which supports the lack of written description conclusions." Id. In addition to identifying the claim limitation at issue, these findings should "[e]stablish a prima facie case by providing reasons why a person skilled in the art at the time the application was filed would not have recognized that the inventor was in possession of the invention as claimed in view of the disclosure of the application as filed." Id.

Although MPEP 2161.01 suggests that "necessary steps and/or flowcharts" may be examples of disclosures having "sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at the time of filing," the MPEP does not establish that these are requirements for establishing a sufficient written description. Thus, a mere assertion that such elements are missing from the specification does not satisfy the Office's initial burden of "presenting by a preponderance of evidence why a person skilled in the art would not recognize in an applicant's disclosure a description of the invention defined by the claims," as required under MPEP § 2163(III)(A).
The Office Action's reliance on Vasudevan Software, Inc. v. MicroStrategy, Inc. (782 F.3d 671, 681-683, 114, USPQ2d 1349, 1356, 1357 (Fed. Cir. 2015)) appears to

be misplaced, in that the Vasudevan court held that there was a genuine issue of material fact whether the specification included sufficient detail, despite finding that the inventor was unable to practice the claimed invention using the software disclosed in the specification, and that the specification lacked a working example. These holdings contradict the assertion in the Office Action that "the specification must explain how the inventor intends to achieve the claimed function."

In fact, the present specification, including at least the disclosures of paragraphs [0035]-[0037] describe the claimed features in sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at the time of filing.
In view of this, Applicant requests that this § 112 rejection be withdrawn. V. Section 112(b) Rejections

In the Office Action, claims 7 and 15 were rejected as allegedly indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) based on the use of the phrase "determining a blood flow characteristic at a location in the non-invasive patient-specific anatomic model" because it was allegedly unclear "if 'a location' is in the original non-invasive patient-specific anatomic model, or the modified non-invasive patient-specific anatomic model." (Office Action at pages 8-10.) While Applicant does not agree that the subject phrase renders claims 7 and 15 unclear, to further prosecution, Applicant amends claims 7 and 15 herein to recite: "determining a blood flow characteristic at a location in the modified non-invasive patient-specific three dimensional anatomic model." This new phrase is clear and definite. Reconsideration of this rejection is requested.

In the Office Action, claims 7 and 15 were rejected as allegedly indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) based on the use of the phrase "generating or displaying a risk score for risk of disease to one or more regions of the patient's bowel, based on the calculated blood flow characteristic at a location in the modified non-invasive patient- specific anatomic model" because it was allegedly unclear "if 'the calculated blood flow characteristic' is the blood flow characteristic from claim 1 or the blood flow characteristic recited in claim 7," and because it was allegedly unclear "if "a location" is the same as, related to, or different from "a location", recited in claim 7, line 4." (Office Action at pages 8-10.) While Applicant does not agree that the subject phrase renders claims 7 and 15 unclear, to further prosecution, Applicant amends claims 7 and 15 herein to recite: "generating or displaying a risk score for risk of disease to one or more regions of the patient's bowel, based on the calculated determined modified blood flow characteristic at [[a]] the location in the modified non-invasive patient-specific three dimensional anatomic model." This new phrase is clear and definite. Reconsideration of this rejection is requested.
VI. Section 101 Rejections

Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection of claims 1029 under 35 U.S.C. § 101 as being directed to non-statutory subject matter. (Office Action at pages 11-20.) In particular, the Office Action asserts that the claims are "drawn to an abstract idea since they involve a mental process that can be practically performed in the human mind including observation, evaluation, judgment, and opinion and using pen and paper." (Office Action at page 12.) Applicant does not agree with the rejection and the characterizations made in the Office Action. Nevertheless, to facilitate prosecution and
without acquiescing to the rejection, the independent claims are amended herein to recite:

p.u: performing a fluid simulation of a blood flow in the received

body.p: calculating a blood flow characteristic of blood delivered to the portion of the patient's bowel using the fluid simulation,
the determined blood flow demand, and a value of
microvascular resistance based on the received
physiological state

The pending claims are not directed to abstract ideas under Step 2(A), prong 1. The subject matter of independent claims 1, 9, and 17 cannot "practically be performed in the human mind." MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2)(III)(A). For example, claims 1, 9, and 17 each recite "performing a fluid simulation of a blood flow in the received patient-specific three dimensional anatomic model" and "calculating a blood flow characteristic of blood delivered to the portion of the patient's bowel using the fluid simulation, the determined blood flow demand, and a value of microvascular resistance based on the received physiological state." The human mind cannot practically perform such simulations or calculate a blood flow characteristic based on the simulations. In particular, the human mind cannot practically perform such simulations or calculations in a "three dimensional anatomic model," as recited by the amended claims. Therefore, the claims are not directed to a mental process.

At least these portions of the amended claims cannot be practically performed in the human mind, as asserted by the Office Action. Accordingly, in view of the foregoing, the rejection of claims 1-20 under § 101 should be withdrawn.
VII. Conclusion

The Office Action contains characterization of the claims and the related art with which the Applicant does not necessarily agree. Unless expressly noted otherwise, Applicant declines to subscribe to any statement or characterization in the Office Action.
In discussing the specification, claims, and drawings in this Reply, it is to be

understood that Applicant is in no way intending to limit the scope of the claims to any exemplary embodiments described in the specification or abstract and/or shown in the drawings. Rather, Applicant is entitled to have the claims interpreted broadly to the maximum extent permitted by statute, regulation, and applicable case law.

In view of the foregoing remarks, Applicant submits that this claimed invention is neither anticipated nor rendered obvious in view of the prior art references cited against this application. Applicant therefore requests the reconsideration and reexamination of the application, and the timely allowance of the pending claims.
